cards.headline: Price tags lie about size.
cards.body: One company's shares cost **$8**. Another's cost **$600**. Which business is bigger? You cannot tell from the price. A share price only reflects how many slices the company cut its ownership into — not how large the company is.

cards.headline: Size has one formula.
cards.body: **Market capitalization** is every share added together: share price times shares outstanding. Northwind trades at **$20** with **50 million** shares, so its market cap is **$1 billion**. That is what the market says the company's equity is worth today.

art.name: market-cap-equation
art.alt: A share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding equals a company's market capitalization.

cards.title: The size ladder
cards.caption: The same word covers wildly different companies. Smaller names can grow faster but swing harder and trade thinly.

cards.prompt: Harbor trades at $600 a share, Cedar at $8. Which company is larger?

options.label: Harbor — its shares cost far more
You cannot tell without the share count

cards.explanation: Price per share depends on how many shares exist. A $600 stock with few shares can be smaller than an $8 stock with billions. Multiply price by share count before judging size.

cards.headline: Buying the whole business.
cards.body: Market cap prices the equity — but a buyer also inherits the company's debts and pockets its cash. **Enterprise value** captures that: market cap plus total debt minus cash. It is the price of the entire operating business, not just its shares.
Picture buying a $500,000 house that carries a $300,000 mortgage and has $50,000 in a safe. Enterprise value is what you truly take on.
Enterprise value starts from market cap, adds the company's [[1]], then subtracts its cash.
cards.explanation: Debt is money the new owner must repay, so it adds to the true price; cash offsets it. Revenue and dividends never enter the calculation.

cards.title: When the pie is cut into more slices
cards.caption: Total profit can rise while each owner's slice shrinks. A climbing share count — often from stock-based pay — dilutes existing holders.

cards.summary: Size, debt and share count frame every other number you will judge.
bullets: Market cap is share price times shares outstanding.
Enterprise value adds debt and subtracts cash.
A rising share count quietly dilutes owners.

art.name: price-vs-value
art.alt: A company's market price sits on one side of a scale and its underlying business value on the other.

cards.insight: Market cap is what the shares cost. Enterprise value is what the business costs. Always know which one you are asking about.
